summary: Pierhead light at the mouth of the Black River, South Haven, Michigan: lit 1872, metal tower of 1903, owned since 2012 by a local historical association.

structures.material: cast iron (archive) or steel plates over metal lath (LighthouseFriends)

staffing.note: Keeper transferred 1940; local Coast Guard station assumed responsibility (LighthouseFriends)

access.note: Not open to the public for tours because of liability concerns; the association opens the lower level for occasional sneak peeks.

facts.agency: Historical Association of South Haven (owner since 2012; formerly U.S. Coast Guard)

events.note: Beacon with a fifth-order lamp on the south pier, per the 1995 federal nomination (citing Ensign's 1880 county history)
Dwelling and pierhead tower completed with a $6,000 appropriation (LighthouseFriends)
Fixed red light first displayed 10 May 1872 (LighthouseFriends). Sources differ on the first date.
Tower moved 120 feet lakeward; gas machine installed inside (LighthouseFriends)
Moved 250 feet to outer end of pier extension, 4 July 1900 (Board report for fiscal 1901). LighthouseFriends dates it 1901 and gives 249 feet.
Metal cylindrical tower replaced the wooden tower; first exhibited 13 November 1903
Fifth-order Fresnel lens (archive, original optic of the 1903 tower)
Hand-operated horn replaced by a 1,200-pound bell, 18 September 1913
Keeper Jesse T. Brown assisted in rescuing two women near the light station (Bulletin 1916; the date is given as 6 July)
Fifty-foot skeletal range tower set up 267 yards shoreward of the pierhead light
Range lights changed from oil to electric illuminant
Elevated walkway relocated from Calumet Light (Illinois) and installed on the pier
Air diaphone sounding two blasts every thirty seconds replaced the fog bell, 25 March 1937
Coast Guard took control of the lighthouses; keeper transferred 1940 and the local Coast Guard station assumed responsibility
Light established on the outer end of the north pier
Piers and revetments listed as Navigation Structures at South Haven Harbor (nomination 1995; amended to add the 1903 north pierhead light)
Coast Guard declared the pierhead light excess to its needs (Notice of Availability, 28 June 2010)
Awarded to the Historical Association of South Haven; deed transfer ceremony 9 August 2012
Interior restored 2015-2016 by Mihm Enterprises; exterior restored with a $60,000 matching grant from the Michigan Lighthouse Assistance Program

keepers.name: Captain William P. Bryan
keepers.note: First keeper. LighthouseFriends says his two years were the shortest tenure of any keeper of the light.

keepers.name: James S. Donahue
keepers.note: Longest-serving keeper (35 years, per LighthouseFriends). Wounded at Wilderness in 1864 (LighthouseFriends). Built a 300-foot handrail in 1880. Logbook records his wife's death, 3 July 1875. Silver medal, 20 May 1890, for rescues from drowning 1875-1889 (Life-Saving Service medal list). Kept the old tower in his yard after 1903.

keepers.name: Jesse T. Brown
keepers.note: Assisted in the 1916 rescue of two women near the light station (Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1916). Bulletin OCR garbles the name; the index and roster give Jesse T. Brown.

wrecks.vessel: Two women (not named in the source)
wrecks.outcome: Keeper Jesse T. Brown assisted in rescuing them from drowning in Lake Michigan near the light station (Lighthouse Service Bulletin, 1916).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends describes a fifth-order Barbier and Fenestre Fresnel lens shown from the first tower on 10 May 1872. The U.S. Lighthouse Society record gives the original optic as a fifth-order Fresnel lens installed in 1903. The story reports both and does not settle the question.

The association's website says the pierhead light is not open to the public for tours, because of liability concerns. The U.S. Lighthouse Society place record says 'Open to Public: Yes', and the record's access level here is 'closed'. The story gives the association's statement, the owner's own words, and notes the Society's record; the record is not corrected here.

LighthouseFriends says two electric flood lights were installed on the outer tower in 1923, when the range lights were changed to electric. A 1924 item in the Lighthouse Service Bulletin describes one electric flood light added on the outside of the front range tower while the illuminant was being changed. The story reports both accounts.

The record's first-lit dates (1872) match LighthouseFriends, which gives a privately maintained beacon on the south pier by 1868 and the Board's first displayed light on 10 May 1872. The federal nomination dates a beacon with a fifth-order lamp on the south pier to 1871, citing an 1880 county history. The story reports the disagreement and does not settle it.

The archive and the nomination describe the 1903 tower as cast iron; LighthouseFriends describes steel plates over metal lath. The 1995 amended items place the 1903 cast-iron light on the north pierhead and a modern light on the south pierhead. The Board's 1901 report and LighthouseFriends place the light station on the south pier. The story follows the Board's report and LighthouseFriends.

The Board's report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1901 gives the move 250 feet to the end of the pier extension on 4 July 1900. LighthouseFriends gives 249 feet in 1901. The story gives the Board's date and notes LighthouseFriends' version.

notes_for_editor: The 1995 NRHP nomination is an engineering nomination for the piers and revetments. Its text on the lights is short, and the amended items are the only account of the 1903 north pierhead light and the modern south pierhead light; those two statements conflict with the Board's 1901 report and with LighthouseFriends, and the story says so. The 1871 beacon comes from the nomination, which cites Ensign's 1880 county history; that history was not read directly. The roster spells the 1909 keeper De Diemar; LighthouseFriends spells him De Diemer. The 1891 medal list is OCR text ('medal.. May 20,1890' and 'ntimber'): quotations are as printed. Keepers were matched by name from the roster. The 1891 medal's award date for Donahue (May 20, 1890) was read by column position in an OCR'd award table: the same date sits beside his name in the 1892 and 1898 medal lists, but the page image was not read. The 1916 Bulletin's keeper name is OCR-garbled ('JcssoT. Brown'); the name is confirmed from the 1912-17 Bulletin index and the roster. The 1880 county history cited by the nomination is Ensign, History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties (1880), known here only through the nomination's citation 'Ensign 1880:46'. LighthouseFriends' flood-light count and lens date, the USLHS 'Open to Public: Yes' entry, and the nomination's 1871 beacon are reported as disagreements in the story. Donahue's Civil War wound, the handrail, the logbook entry and the old tower in his yard rest on LighthouseFriends alone; the logbook entry is quoted through LighthouseFriends, which is copyrighted, as one short sentence. The 1916 Bulletin gives the rescue date as 6 July without a year in the sentence; the year is taken from the 1916 issue. Chronicling America searches for the 1890-91 medal and the 1903 tower returned no hits, so newspapers were not used. Owner and operator of the light are named because they are public organisations, not private residents.
